title: I can’t say it Bloom me away #theatre #literature #ulysses #experimen...
transcript: The same people who did the 8 hour long Great Gatsby stage show are now doing James Joyce's Ulysses. But this one is much more abridged, which is probably smart, but it does beg the question if it's possible to successfully adapt such an unwieldy novel into a three hour stage production? Well, they definitely did it, but not successfully, in my opinion. The way the show is conceived is that it's almost like a table read that gets more chaotic as it goes along. And instead of doing every word of the novel like they did with Great Gatsby, they do this fast-forward effect every time they skip over or cut something. All of that is very interesting on paper, and I do like the whole ethos behind this theatre company, Elevator Repair Service, in terms of repurposing existing text in direct ways for the stage. I think I also understand why they made the choices they did where they were trying to put the text front and center and give us an abridged version of it, while still conveying the scope and structure of this epic story told over the course of one day. But I think it backfired in a couple ways: This whole fast-forward device was a clever idea, but it was constantly disrupting and resetting the flow of each scene. The scenes felt like they were kind of gasping for air, and I, as the audience member, felt like I was constantly losing my foothold every 30 seconds. That, plus the breakneck speed, the non-literal staging, the limited attempts to reinterpret or editorialize it, and the already inscrutable nature of James Joyce's source material just made it really frustrating and hard to follow. And you might say, well, Ulysses *is* frustrating and hard to follow. That's just the nature of the book. And maybe I'm to blame for not doing my homework, but even though I haven't read Ulysses, I *imagine* it's more rewarding on the page because the reader can engage with it at their own pace and with a greater sense of agency. But the comparatively passive experience of having it delivered to you while sitting in a theatre, is a lot less rewarding and maybe even more challenging, in a certain sense. It seems to me that by trying to be so deferential to James Joyce's writing, they ended up doing the opposite; by putting it on stage without tailoring it to the storytelling demands of the medium of theatre. James Joyce is kind of left out to dry because they put his work in a context that doesn't cast it in a flattering light. But if you're curious to see this admittedly valiant attempt for yourself, it's running at the Public Theater in New York City until March 1st.
